spine: 1. SAML 誕生於 2002 年，由 Netegrity、Securant、VeriSign、Jamcracker 四家廠商各自的 XML 安全提案（S2ML、AuthXML、X-TASS、ITML）合併進 OASIS 標準——規格書的體積，從一開始就是好幾份提案疊出來的，不是單一團隊精簡設計的結果，這是後面「規格避開九成」量化說法的背景。
2. SAML 用的是 enveloped signature：Signature 元素直接插進被簽的 Assertion 內部；JWT 用的是 detached signature，靠一個句點把簽章跟內容分開。
3. 簽章驗證要靠 canonicalization 先把 XML 轉成一致的位元組序列，SP 與 IdP 只要對「等價」的判斷有一絲落差，簽章就對不上；而簽章又嵌在被修改的資料裡，要同時改資料又維持 byte-for-byte 等價表示，原文說「it is very difficult」。
4. 核心論點（貫穿 H2 3 與全文結尾）：XSW 攻擊利用的不是密碼學漏洞，而是「簽章驗證認可的元素」跟「應用邏輯實際讀取的元素」不保證是同一個——驗證器可以誠實回報簽章正確，應用程式讀到的卻是另一段內容。
5. 這個落差原文稱其為「the proverbial arrow to SAML's heel」：2012 年「On Breaking SAML」論文把攻擊方法系統化、自動化，13 年後的 2025 年，libxml2、parser differential 等新變種還在被公開揭露。
6. OIDC 走的是完全不同的路：建立在 HTTP 之上，簽章 detached，而且靠一串漸進的 RFC（PKCE 2015、行動版 2017、device grant 2019、DPoP 2023）持續長大；SAML 幾乎一次把功能寫進 2002 年的規格，之後沒怎麼進化。
7. 作者給新接 SSO 的 SP 的建議很直接：「Just support OIDC. Abandon SAML.」；給既有、走不開的 SP 的建議來自 Ptacek——額外檢查訊息形狀像不像 Okta、Onelogin、Google、Shibboleth；給 IdP 的建議則是排時程、停收新客戶、備好對應 OIDC 設定、設 sunset date。

perspective.mechanism: SAML's enveloped XML signature (the Signature element sits inside the very Assertion it signs) forces every verification through canonicalization — a byte-level agreement between SP and IdP about what the XML 'means' — and any gap between the element a validator cryptographically checks and the element application logic actually parses opens the door to XML Signature Wrapping (XSW): a decoy element gets consumed while a genuinely-signed element elsewhere satisfies the validator.
perspective.tradeoff: SAML's transport independence and up-front kitchen-sink specification were reasonable choices for the disconnected-network, pre-HTTP-dominant world of 2002, but the same choices now mean ~90% of the spec goes unused per deployment while the enveloped-signature/canonicalization core keeps producing new parser-differential bypasses (2018, 2025) that a JSON/HTTP-native, detached-signature protocol like OIDC structurally avoids.
perspective.reader_use: An engineer maintaining a SAML SP this week can narrow the SAML message shape it accepts to match known-good IdPs (Okta/Onelogin/Google/Shibboleth) as an interim tightening, while treating full OIDC migration as the actual fix for new integrations; an engineer building new SSO support should default to OIDC and skip SAML integration entirely.

notes.quote: In the JWT example above, the blue signature is detached from the JSON payload and delimited in the JWT with a period ('.'). In the SAML example, the Signature element is inserted ('enveloped') in the Assertion element.
notes.interpretation: The structural core distinction between SAML and JWT: SAML's signature lives inside the data it authenticates; JWT keeps them separate.

notes.quote: if the SP and IdP cannot agree on a consistent representation of the XML data, then the bytes won't line up, the signatures won't match, and your authentication fails.
notes.interpretation: Explains why canonicalization (C14N) exists and why it's fragile: signature verification requires byte-identical serialization, and any parser disagreement about equivalence breaks auth.

notes.quote: What's insidious about SAML is that it really is mostly straightforward to understand, but it's built on a foundation of sand, bone dust, and ash
notes.interpretation: Thomas Ptacek's framing quote, used by the author as the article's guiding thesis: SAML looks simple but rests on a fragile foundation.

notes.quote: it works … if you assume XML signature validation is reliable. But XML signature validation is deeply cursed.
notes.interpretation: Continuation of the Ptacek framing: SAML's apparent simplicity depends on an unreliable premise (XML signature validation).

notes.quote: XML signature wrapping (XSW) attacks are the proverbial arrow to SAML's heel.
notes.interpretation: Names XSW as the flagship/most consequential attack class stemming from the enveloped-signature + canonicalization design.

notes.quote: I consider the godfather of it all to be 'On Breaking SAML: Be Whoever You Want to Be' (2012). It tested theory against practice and resulted in an automated way to check for XSW attacks.
notes.interpretation: Dates the systematization of XSW attack methodology to a specific 2012 paper that produced automated detection tooling.

notes.quote: Canonicalization bugs enabled Kelby's XML comment bypass in 2018: ... I was there when Kelby Ludwig found the XML comment bypass
notes.interpretation: Names a specific, dated (2018) real-world exploit of canonicalization bugs, attributed to Kelby Ludwig (full surname given elsewhere in the article), as a concrete instance of the class. The article gives no mechanism detail beyond naming the bug.

notes.quote: PKCE published via RFC 7636 (2015), PKCE for mobile/native apps published via RFC 8252 (2017), Device authorization grant for IoT devices published via RFC 8628 (2019), Demonstrating proof of possession (DPoP) for MFA workflows published via RFC 9449 (2023)
notes.interpretation: Lists OIDC's incremental, dated RFC extensions, used to contrast with SAML's up-front, non-iterating design model.

notes.quote: OpenID Connect 1.0 specification published (2014)
notes.interpretation: Anchors OIDC's own base specification to 2014, the historical starting point for its incremental RFC evolution.

notes.quote: Abusing libxml2 quirks to bypass SAML authentication on GitHub Enterprise (2025), Sign in as anyone: Bypassing SAML SSO authentication with parser differentials (2025), SAML roulette: the hacker always wins (2025), The Fragile Lock: Novel Bypasses For SAML Authentication (2025)
notes.interpretation: CORRECTED after Step 7.6c: these four are listed by the article under Canonicalization as parser-differential/round-trip bugs (the article's own framing, see n28), not explicitly as instances of 'the same XSW class named in 2012' for all four. Only The Fragile Lock is explicitly linked to XSW via n29 ('XSW is still present today', hyperlinked to that piece). Two of the four ('SAML roulette' and 'The Fragile Lock') are both published by PortSwigger Research in 2025 (see n30) — not four independent teams.

notes.quote: The problem here is that it is very difficult to get a byte-for-byte, canonically equivalent representation of the data when you're also modifying it!
notes.interpretation: Explains specifically why enveloped signatures compound the canonicalization problem: modifying signed data while preserving byte-level canonical equivalence is inherently hard.

notes.quote: So what can I do if I'm a service provider (i.e., SP) and I'd like to integrate into the SSO ecosystem without SAML? Just support OIDC. Abandon SAML.
notes.interpretation: The author's direct, primary recommendation for engineers building new SP-side SSO integrations.

notes.quote: We've managed to hold the line on OIDC so far. So has Tailscale. If Tailscale can hold the line...
notes.interpretation: CORRECTED after Step 7.6c: this is a blockquote the article attributes to Thomas Ptacek (2024), not Schwager's own words — 'we' refers to Ptacek's company (Fly.io), not necessarily Trail of Bits. Still concrete evidence that avoiding SAML is operationally viable for a real SP, but the attribution in prose must name Ptacek/Fly.io, not 'the author's own company'.

notes.quote: Remember, as a vendor, you're often competing with companies that don't do real SSO integration at all.
notes.interpretation: Extends n12/n13: the competitive argument for why an SP can afford to skip SAML — many competitors don't do real SSO integration either, so OIDC-only support is still competitive.

notes.quote: develop a deprecation plan, communicate it to customers, stop onboarding new customers to SAML integrations, provide existing SAML customers with equivalent OIDC configurations, set a sunset date...
notes.interpretation: The author's staged-deprecation checklist aimed at identity providers (IdPs), distinct audience/advice from the SP recommendation.

notes.quote: the following intellectual property was contributed to the SSTC: Security Services Markup Language (S2ML) from Netegrity; AuthXML from Securant; XML Trust Assertion Service Specification (X-TASS) from VeriSign; Information Technology Markup Language (ITML) from Jamcracker
notes.interpretation: SAML's origin as a merger of four separate, competing vendor XML security proposals in 2002 — explains the 'kitchen sink' spec bloat as baked in from inception.

notes.quote: SAML is an XML-based markup language for security assertions. It was created in 2002 by the Organization for the Advancement of Structured Information Standards (OASIS).
notes.interpretation: Basic definitional/historical fact establishing what SAML is and when/by whom it was created.

notes.quote: JSON was 'discovered' in 2001, but this was right around the time the SAML committee was meeting
notes.interpretation: Contrasts SAML's XML foundation with the near-simultaneous emergence of JSON, used to argue the format choice looks worse in hindsight.

notes.quote: OIDC assumes HTTP, whereas SAML is transport independent.
notes.interpretation: Names one concrete ossification axis: SAML's transport independence, a historical asset, becomes complexity baggage once HTTP+TLS is universal.

notes.quote: 99% of modern SAML implementations use a very similar data shape and subset of the specification.
notes.interpretation: Supports the over-specification argument: real deployments converge on a narrow subset of the full spec surface, per the author's own estimate.

notes.quote: SAML had a good 25 year run.
notes.interpretation: The article's closing editorial framing: SAML's era, while genuinely functional for a long stretch, is now over.

notes.quote: If I was adding SAML support to something new, I'd consider beyond all the standard SAML checks also rejecting any message that doesn't have the same shape as what Okta, Onelogin, Google, or Shib generates.
notes.interpretation: CORRECTED after Step 7.6c: the quote's own scope is explicitly 'adding SAML support to something new' (a new integration), not maintaining an existing SP. The prose must preserve this conditional and mark any application of the idea to an existing, already-deployed SAML SP as this post's extension, not Ptacek's/the article's stated scope. Presented as 'I'd consider', a personal suggestion rather than a firm claim — kept hedged in prose.

notes.quote: Any given SAML authentication you would encounter in the wild today probably avoids 90% of the specification.
notes.interpretation: Kitchen-sink specification claim: most real deployments use only a small fraction of SAML's full spec surface. Note 'probably' and 'any given' (per-authentication, not per-deployment) hedges must be preserved in prose.

notes.quote: But XML signature validation is deeply cursed, and is so complicated that most fielded SAML implementations are wrapping libxmlsec, a gnarly C codebase nobody reads.
notes.interpretation: The article's own stated consequence of 'deeply cursed' XML signature validation: most real SAML implementations end up wrapping libxmlsec, a complex, little-read C codebase. This is the source's actual causal claim — not a general statement that canonicalization is 'easy to get wrong'.

notes.quote: SAML came about at a time when HTTP + TLS was not yet the dominant backbone of web service communication, and it has never reconciled with this modern landscape.
notes.interpretation: The article's actual framing of SAML's transport-independence ossification: it doesn't call transport independence an 'advantage' at the time, only that SAML predates HTTP+TLS dominance and has 'never reconciled' with the modern landscape since.

notes.quote: SAML failed to anticipate the mobile, SPA, and IoT revolutions, and had no answers when these technologies arrived on the scene in the late aughts.
notes.interpretation: The article's stated claim about SAML and mobile/SPA/IoT: SAML failed to anticipate these technologies and had no answers when they arrived — it does not say these scenarios 'mostly default to HTTPS now', that framing is not in the source.

notes.quote: OIDC grew organically over the years, whereas SAML was largely designed up front.
notes.interpretation: The article's actual OIDC-vs-SAML evolution contrast: 'largely designed up front', not 'entirely/all at once' — a softer claim than the post previously stated.

notes.quote: SAML was designed in a different era for a different time and has not received necessary updates.
notes.interpretation: The article's stated claim: SAML 'has not received necessary updates', not that it 'has no iteration mechanism at all' — the post's earlier wording overstated the absoluteness of this.

notes.quote: Canonicalization is often a precursor to parser differential and/or 'round-trip' bugs, which are what most modern SAML attacks use:
notes.interpretation: The article's own framing for the list of 2020-2025 items that follows (including the four 2025 items): they are canonicalization-adjacent parser-differential/round-trip bugs, not individually asserted to each be 'the XSW class named in 2012'. Note 'often' hedge.

notes.quote: Despite being front and center in this 2012 paper, XSW is still present today.
notes.interpretation: The article's explicit XSW-persistence claim is hyperlinked specifically to 'The Fragile Lock' (PortSwigger, 2025), not generally to all four 2025 items listed under canonicalization/parser-differential bugs.

notes.quote: [SAML roulette: the hacker always wins](https://portswigger.net/research/saml-roulette-the-hacker-always-wins) (2025) / [The Fragile Lock: Novel Bypasses For SAML Authentication](https://portswigger.net/research/the-fragile-lock) (2025)
notes.interpretation: Two of the four 2025 items cited in the article ('SAML roulette' and 'The Fragile Lock') are both published by PortSwigger Research, confirmed via re-fetch of the linked bylines — they are not four independently-authored disclosures.

notes.quote: This adds significant complexity for largely unused features.
notes.interpretation: The article's own stated conclusion from the 90%/99% figures is that unused spec surface ADDS complexity — the opposite of a 'narrower attack surface' framing. Any 'narrower attack surface therefore shape-checking is feasible' argument must be marked as this post's own extension, not the source's conclusion.
